evidence.claim: Granite battle markers and Chickasaw history along rural Mississippi roads
evidence.quote: Granite markers along Highway 370 describe the battle where Gen. Nathan Bedford Forrest and General Sturgis met in battle June 10, 1864.

evidence.claim: Granite battle markers and Chickasaw history along rural Mississippi roads
evidence.quote: Highway 370, Highway 348, CR 833 and CR 503 are rural routes with a rich history of civil war, Indian culture and early settlements of the area.

evidence.claim: The Brice’s Crossroads Battlefield-Chief Tishomingo route links Baldwyn and Guntown through country that is largely rural and agricultural.
evidence.quote: Most of the remainder of the route with the exception of the last half mile portion within Guntown is rural and primarily agricultural.

evidence.claim: Granite markers along Highway 370 explain the battle fought here on June 10, 1864.
evidence.quote: Granite markers along Highway 370 describe the battle where Gen. Nathan Bedford Forrest and General Sturgis met in battle June 10, 1864.

evidence.claim: The corridor management plan makes its case for scenic-byway designation through Civil War, Native American and early African American histories in a rural landscape.
evidence.quote: Histories derived from the Civil War, the Native Americans and early African Americans, culminating into a historically rich area with a naturally scenic backdrop.

evidence.claim: The driving route grew from battlefield preservation and interpretation.
evidence.quote: Much of the proposed Byway already has established tourist stops of historic value

evidence.claim: A state grant, artifacts donated by the Claude Gentry family and land donated by the Haynes family helped establish the interpretive center, which opened in 1998.
evidence.quote: With initial funding of a quarter of a million dollars educational Enhancement Grant from the state legislature, the donation of the artifacts from the previous museum from the Claude Gentry family and a donation of 12 acres by the Haynes family of Baldwyn, The 2800 sq. ft. Brice’s’ Crossroads Visitor and Interpretive Center opened in 1998.

evidence.claim: Identification of Chief Tishomingo’s home site led organizers to extend the proposed byway to include it and other Chickasaw historical sites.
evidence.quote: This resulted in the extension of the proposed Byway to include Tishomingo’s home site and marker along with several other Chickasaw historical sites

evidence.claim: Chickasaw Governor Bill Anoatubby supported the designation effort.
evidence.quote: Chickasaw Governor Bill Anoatubby has sent an official letter of Support from the Chickasaw Nation for the designation

evidence.claim: The planned journey begins at the interpretive center on Grisham Street in Baldwyn and follows MS 370 toward the battlefield.
evidence.quote: Starting at the Brice’s Crossroads Visitors and Interpretive Center which is mile post 0.00, go along Grisham Street to the intersection of MS 370.

evidence.claim: The national battlefield site lies west of Baldwyn on Highway 370.
evidence.quote: It is located about 6 miles (10 km) west of Baldwyn, on Highway 370.

evidence.claim: County Roads 833 and 503 then lead to MS 348 at Blair, with the route ending at MS 145 in Guntown.
evidence.quote: Then go along MS 370 to CR 833 to CR 503, then along CR 503 to MS 348 at the Blair Community, turn left and continue Hwy. 348, to Mississippi Highway 145 which is the terminus of the byway and milepost 12.8.

evidence.claim: A one-acre grassy park marks the place where the Brice family house stood.
evidence.quote: The 1-acre site is a grassy park

evidence.claim: It contains a flagpole, a memorial monument and two cannons.
evidence.quote: with a flagpole, a memorial monument, and two cannons.

evidence.claim: Here, on June 10, 1864, Nathan Bedford Forrest’s smaller Confederate force defeated a U.S. Army force.
evidence.quote: a U.S. Army force was defeated by a smaller Confederate force commanded by Major-General Nathan Bedford Forrest on June 10, 1864

evidence.claim: The neighboring Old Bethany Cemetery contains the graves of more than 90 Confederate soldiers killed in the battle.
evidence.quote: The graves of more than 90 Confederate soldiers killed in the battle are also located in this cemetery.

evidence.claim: U.S. Army dead were first buried in common graves on the battlefield and later reinterred in Memphis National Cemetery.
evidence.quote: U.S. Army soldiers killed in the battle were buried in common graves on the battlefield but were later reinterred in the Memphis National Cemetery at Memphis, Tennessee.

evidence.claim: The modern Bethany church occupies a different site from the congregation’s wartime meeting house.
evidence.quote: The modern Bethany Presbyterian Church is located on the southeast side of the crossroads. At the time of the battle, this congregation's meeting house was located further south along Baldwyn Road.

evidence.claim: A one-acre grassy park marks the place where the Brice family house stood.
evidence.quote: This is the spot where the Brice family house once stood.

evidence.claim: The wartime bridge over Tishomingo Creek became a bottleneck during the Union retreat.
evidence.quote: this retreat bottlenecked at the Tishomingo bridge

evidence.claim: Abandoned wagons and dead pack animals blocked the crossing, and many Federal soldiers tried to swim or ford the creek under Confederate fire.
evidence.quote: Abandoned wagons and dead pack animals blocked the bridge, leading many Federal troops to swim or ford the creek, at which point they were shot down in large numbers by the Confederates.

evidence.claim: A later pedestrian bridge was built at the location of that crossing.
evidence.quote: The New Pedestrian Bridge Over Tishomingo Creek This gives Civil War enthusiast the ability to stand in the exact location of the bridge that existed here during the battle

evidence.claim: The creek bears Chief Tishomingo’s name, and the Chickasaw Nation honors him with his image at the center of its national seal.
evidence.quote: Tishomingo was and is so respected by the Chickasaw Nation he is honored by his image being placed in the center of the National Seal of the Chickasaw Nation.

evidence.claim: The creek bears Chief Tishomingo’s name
evidence.quote: the creek named in honor of their most respected chiefs, Chief Tishomingo

evidence.claim: Guntown’s older streets lie east of Highway 145 near the railroad tracks.
evidence.quote: Guntown is located along Highway 145, with the older parts of the city lying further to the east near the railroad tracks.

evidence.claim: During the Civil War, United States Cavalry officers described it as a station and small village on the Mobile & Ohio railroad.
evidence.quote: During the American Civil War, United States Cavalry officers described it as "a station and small village on the Mobile & Ohio road."

evidence.claim: The town was incorporated in 1867.
evidence.quote: it was initially incorporated as the "Town of Guntown" on February 16, 1867.

evidence.claim: Its name reaches further back, to Virginia loyalist James G. Gunn, who found asylum among the Chickasaw in what is now Lee County.
evidence.quote: Guntown is named for Virginia loyalist émigré James G. Gunn (d. 1826) who found asylum among the Chickasaw in present-day Lee County.

evidence.claim: The corridor also includes Chickasaw home sites on Reynoldsburg Road, which the Chickasaws built partly with U.S. government funds as an alternative to the Natchez Trace into middle Tennessee.
evidence.quote: A road built with in part with funds from the US government by the Chickasaws to give travelers an alternate to the Natchez Trace to middle Tennessee.

evidence.claim: The corridor also includes Chickasaw home sites on Reynoldsburg Road, which the Chickasaws built partly with U.S. government funds as an alternative to the Natchez Trace into middle Tennessee.
evidence.quote: Both these Chickasaw home sites were located on the Reynoldsburg road.

evidence.claim: At the nearby overlook, Forrest directed Confederate cannon forward to fire without infantry support during the battle.
evidence.quote: From this overlook, Gen. Nathan B. Forrest commanded his troops to advance the Confederate cannon to the front, and fire without infantry support.

flags: The only official cache is a corridor plan that repeatedly calls the byway proposed. Current designation and designation date are not independently established; the overview describes the designation effort.
The plan gives a 12.8-mile route; material gives 15.4 mapped miles and a Guntown strip mile of 13.62. Mileage omitted pending map review.

The plan documents a pedestrian bridge and trails at Tishomingo Creek but predates this review. Current access and bridge condition are unverified; no present-access promise or practical note supplied.
National Register date conflicts: the plan says 1976 while the battlefield article says 1966. Omitted; preserved acreage also varies by source and date.
Guntown and Tishomingo Creek moments are shorter than the target because the relevant evidence supports compact narratives.
